segments.sec: Start Here: Foundations
segments.say: Lesson 1. What is D S A & How to Solve Any Problem. What data structures and algorithms actually are, the map of everything ahead, and a 6-step method for cracking any problem.

segments.sec: The basics
segments.say: A data structure is a way of arranging data in memory (a list, a dictionary, a tree. ). An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe that works on that data. D S A interviews check whether you can pick the right pair to solve a problem quickly. Here is an analogy. Think of a kitchen. Where you store things (spice rack, fridge, drawers) is the data structure. The recipe is the algorithm. A good cook keeps the salt where the recipe needs it, and a good engineer stores data where the algorithm can reach it fast.

segments.sec: The basics
segments.say: Why does this matter? Almost every software interview (internal moves and product companies) has 1–2 D S A rounds. It trains you to think about speed and memory before writing code. You'll see the same ~15 patterns again and again, so learning patterns beats memorizing 500 problems. A few key words. Input / Output: What the function receives, and what it must return. Constraints: Limits like "n less than or equal to 10 to the 5". They tell you how fast your solution must be. Edge case: Unusual input that breaks naive code: empty list, one element, duplicates, negatives. Brute force: The obvious, try-everything solution. Usually correct but slow. Time complexity: How the number of steps grows as input grows (Big-O, next lesson). Pattern: A reusable trick that solves a whole family of problems (two pointers, sliding window. ).

segments.sec: Watch: The 6-step method for any problem
segments.say: The 6-step method for any problem. Understand: repeat the problem in your own words. Ask: what's the input type? Can it be empty? Negative numbers? Duplicates? What exactly do I return?

segments.sec: Watch: The 6-step method for any problem
segments.say: Examples: work 1–2 tiny examples by hand, including one tricky case. This is where most "aha" moments happen.

segments.sec: Watch: The 6-step method for any problem
segments.say: Brute force: say the obvious solution out loud even if it's slow, and state its Big-O. Interviewers want to see you can get a working answer.

segments.sec: Watch: The 6-step method for any problem
segments.say: Optimize: what work is repeated? Could a hash map, sorting, two pointers or a window avoid it? This is where the patterns in this app come in.

segments.sec: Watch: The 6-step method for any problem
segments.say: Code: write it cleanly with good variable names, talking through it as you go.

segments.sec: Watch: The 6-step method for any problem
segments.say: Test: trace your own example through the code line by line, then try the edge cases. Fix bugs before the interviewer finds them.

segments.sec: Watch: Your first algorithm, step by step: find the largest number
segments.say: Your first algorithm, step by step: find the largest number. An algorithm is just precise steps. Goal: return the largest number in the list. Watch the highlighted code line on the right as each step runs.

segments.say: Start by assuming the first number is the biggest: best equals 3.

segments.say: Loop: x equals 8. Is 8 greater than 3? Yes, so update best equals 8.

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: The map: data structures you will learn. Array / list: items in a row, numbered 0, 1, 2. String: a row of characters. Hash map (dict) / set: instant lookup by key. Stack / queue: last-in-first-out / first-in-first-out lines. Linked list: items chained by pointers. Tree: hierarchy with a root and children. Heap: always gives you the smallest (or largest) item fast. Graph: nodes connected by edges (maps, networks).

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: The map: algorithm patterns you will learn. Two pointers, sliding window, prefix sum, binary search: array tricks. Recursion, D F S, B F S: exploring trees and graphs. Backtracking: try all choices smartly. Dynamic programming: remember answers to sub-problems. Greedy: take the best local choice when it's safe.

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: How to practice (15-minute blocks). Watch the pattern animation until you could explain it to a friend. Read each problem and try the brute force in your head first. Learn the smart way, then close the solution and code it yourself. Revisit with the Recall cards and boss battles a few days later. Spaced repetition is what makes it stick.

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: Say it in the interview. "Let me make sure I understand: the input is., I return. Can the list be empty? Let me try a small example. The brute force would be., which is O of n squared. I think we can do better by. ".

segments.sec: Compare
segments.say: Data structure cheat sheet. Array / list: numbered lockers, reading by index O of 1, inserting in the middle O of n. Hash map / set: a dictionary with an instant index, lookup by key O of 1, keeping order, sorting. Stack: a pile of plates, push/pop the top O of 1, reaching the bottom. Queue: a ticket line, add back, remove front O of 1, random access. Linked list: a treasure hunt of clues, insert/remove at a known node O of 1, finding the k-th item O of n. Heap: a V I P line, get min/max O of 1, push/pop O of log n, searching arbitrary items. Tree / B S T: a family tree, search in sorted tree O of log n, gets slow if unbalanced. Graph: a road map, modelling connections, needs B F S/D F S to explore.

segments.sec: Interview recall
segments.say: A likely interview question: How do you approach a coding problem you've never seen? A strong answer: Clarify the inputs and outputs, work small examples, state a brute force with its complexity, look for repeated work and the matching pattern, code cleanly, then test with my examples and edge cases.
